title: Lightweight Swarm Communication for Drones & Robots
description: Explore Pilot Protocol for drone swarms and robot fleets: a lightweight daemon, direct-path preference, and encrypted relay fallback.
seoTitle: Lightweight Swarm Communication for Drones & Robots
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: Robotics teams building multi-robot swarms on ROS2 run into a recurring scaling problem. DDS, the middleware underneath ROS2, uses multicast for peer discovery. On WiFi networks -- where most mobile robots and drones actually operate -- multicast is unreliable, generates broadcast storms, and consumes bandwidth that the robots need for telemetry and coordination. The result: adding more robots to the swarm makes communication worse, not better.

The question robotics teams keep asking is straightforward: what affordable, stable system provides communication between multiple robots without the overhead of ROS2/DDS? This article examines why the DDS multicast model breaks for swarms, what lightweight alternatives exist, and how a single-socket UDP overlay with registry-based discovery can coordinate robot swarms on constrained hardware.

ROS2 uses DDS (Data Distribution Service) as its communication middleware. DDS was designed for military and industrial systems where participants are on the same wired LAN with reliable multicast support. It works well in that environment. The problems start when you move to WiFi, cellular, or mixed networks -- which is where most modern robot swarms actually operate.

DDS uses SPDP (Simple Participant Discovery Protocol) to find other participants on the network. Each participant periodically multicasts its presence. With 10 robots, that is 10 discovery messages every few seconds, each broadcast to all network participants. On WiFi, multicast frames are transmitted at the lowest data rate (often 1 Mbps on 802.11b/g compatibility mode), consuming disproportionate airtime. With 50 robots, the discovery traffic alone can saturate the WiFi channel.

The ROS2 middleware layer -- type support, serialization, executor callbacks -- adds delay to every message on top of raw DDS. For a swarm doing position updates at 10 Hz, that delay makes the position data each robot receives staler than it needs to be.

WiFi access points handle multicast by converting it to broadcast, which is transmitted without acknowledgment or retransmission. If a robot misses a multicast frame due to interference (common in outdoor environments with 2.4 GHz congestion), the message is silently lost. DDS has reliability mechanisms, but they depend on the transport layer delivering the multicast in the first place. On WiFi, this assumption fails routinely.

A ROS2 node with DDS middleware carries memory and CPU overhead that grows with the number of topics and participants. On a Raspberry Pi 4 or a Jetson Nano that is also running a navigation stack, vision processing, and motor control, that overhead competes with the robot's real work. Every megabyte matters when you are running neural networks on edge hardware.
Why Swarms Need Something Lighter Than ROS2
Robot swarms have specific communication requirements that differ from single-robot ROS2 systems:

Every robot needs to share its state (position, battery, task status) with every other robot. This is not point-to-point; it is a broadcast pattern. But it needs to work on WiFi, where real broadcast is unreliable.
Drones on cellular, ground robots on WiFi, the ground station on ethernet. The communication system must bridge these networks without requiring all participants to be on the same LAN.
Swarm robots are cost-optimized. They run on Raspberry Pi, Jetson Nano, ESP32, or similarly constrained platforms. The communication stack cannot consume a large share of RAM or a full CPU core.
Robots join when powered on, leave when battery dies, and may rejoin later. The system must handle this without manual reconfiguration.
Swarms operate in warehouses, agricultural fields, disaster zones, and construction sites. There is no IT department to configure routers, open ports, or manage certificates.

ROS2/DDS was not designed for these constraints. It was designed for fixed installations with wired networks and powerful compute nodes. Using it for swarms works in the lab (where the WiFi is clean and the robot count is small) but fails in the field.
Pilot's Approach: Single Socket, No Multicast, Registry Discovery
Pilot Protocol takes a fundamentally different approach to the problems DDS struggles with.

Each Pilot daemon uses one UDP socket for all communication. There is no multicast, no broadcast, no SPDP discovery traffic. All messages are unicast -- sent directly from one peer to another. On WiFi, unicast frames are transmitted at the highest negotiated data rate with acknowledgment and retransmission. This means every Pilot message gets the reliability that WiFi provides for unicast, which multicast discards.

Instead of multicast discovery, robots register with a registry server under a hostname and can label themselves with up to three tags. Other robots look a peer up by hostname to get its virtual address. The registry (with its companion beacon) can be the public one run by Vulture Labs, or your own on the ground station or a cloud VM. Discovery traffic is unicast TCP to the registry, not multicast on the WiFi channel.

fields.code:
# Each drone registers a name and labels itself on startup
pilotctl set-hostname drone-07
pilotctl extras set-tags drone survey-team-alpha quadcopter  # max 3 tags

# Ground station resolves a drone it trusts (or shares a network with)
pilotctl find drone-07

# The drone's tags come back with a registry lookup
pilotctl --json lookup drone-07

Architecture: Drone Swarm Coordinating via Event Stream

Here is a concrete architecture for a swarm of 10 survey drones coordinated by a ground station. Every Pilot daemon runs an event-stream broker on port 1002; the swarm shares the broker of one always-on hub node. Each drone publishes telemetry (position, battery, status) to the hub. The ground station subscribes to all telemetry, computes the survey plan, and publishes waypoints back to individual drones.

Field deployments introduce a network topology that lab setups do not have. Drones connect via cellular (4G/5G), ground robots via WiFi, and the ground station via a wired connection or a different WiFi network. These networks assign private IPs behind NAT, and the participants cannot directly reach each other.
Pilot handles this transparently with its three-stage NAT traversal:
Each drone discovers its public IP and port by querying the beacon server over UDP.

When a direct packet does not get through, the beacon coordinates a simultaneous hole-punch. Both peers send a UDP packet to each other's public endpoint at the same time, creating NAT mappings that allow bidirectional traffic. This works through the cone-type NATs common on consumer and carrier networks.

When hole-punching fails (symmetric NAT, common on enterprise networks and some cellular carriers), the beacon relays the encrypted traffic. That adds a trip through the beacon, and it works as long as both peers can reach the beacon.

fields.code:
# Drone on cellular (behind carrier-grade NAT)
pilotctl daemon start
# Direct path first, then hole-punch, then relay -- tried automatically
# No configuration needed on the drone

# Ground station on WiFi (behind home router NAT)
pilotctl daemon start
# Same: automatic NAT traversal

# Once they trust each other, both can communicate whatever the NAT
pilotctl ping 0:0000.0002.0001  # Ground station pings drone

children.text: This is critical for field deployment. You do not ask a farmer to configure port forwarding on the cellular modem attached to a survey drone. You do not ask a search-and-rescue team to set up a VPN before deploying robots in a disaster zone. The communication just works because NAT traversal is built into the protocol, not bolted on as a configuration step.
Comparison: Pilot vs ROS2/DDS vs MAVLink vs Zenoh

has the largest ecosystem. If you need MoveIt for manipulation, Nav2 for navigation, or integration with hundreds of sensor drivers, ROS2 is the pragmatic choice despite its communication overhead. The communication layer is the price you pay for the ecosystem.

is purpose-built for drone autopilots. It is extremely lightweight and well-suited for telemetry and command between a ground station and drones using standard autopilot firmware (ArduPilot, PX4). But it is point-to-point and has no pub/sub, no encryption, and no NAT traversal. For swarm coordination beyond basic telemetry, you need something on top of MAVLink.

is the closest competitor for this use case. It has low overhead, supports pub/sub, and has a router-based approach to bridging networks. Its scouting mechanism still uses multicast by default (though it can be configured for unicast), and its NAT traversal relies on Zenoh routers rather than built-in hole-punching. For constrained environments, Zenoh is a strong option.

occupies the niche of zero-configuration swarm communication. No multicast, built-in NAT traversal, static binaries, and encrypted by default. It trades the rich QoS model of DDS for simplicity and the massive ecosystem of ROS2 for lightweight deployment.
Honesty about limitations matters more than feature lists. Pilot is not suitable for everything in robotics:

Pilot uses UDP with congestion control and flow control, but it does not provide deterministic latency. For safety-critical control loops -- motor commands, emergency stops, collision avoidance at 100+ Hz -- you need a real-time transport like EtherCAT, ROS2 with real-time Linux, or direct serial communication. Pilot is for coordination (telemetry, task assignment, swarm planning), not for actuator control.

DDS provides configurable QoS: reliable vs best-effort, transient-local vs volatile, deadline constraints, liveliness assertions. Pilot's event stream has none of these: events travel over the daemon's reliable stream, but nothing is stored, so a subscriber that is disconnected when an event is published never receives it. For telemetry at 10 Hz (where the next update replaces the previous one), this is acceptable. For critical commands, use
(the data exchange port, 1001), where the receiver acknowledges each message it stores.

Unlike DDS's decentralized multicast discovery, Pilot uses a registry for peer discovery. If the network is temporarily unreachable, new robots cannot discover peers, but existing connections continue working.

Pilot does not provide a ROS2 transport plugin. If your robot stack depends on ROS2 packages (Nav2, MoveIt, sensor drivers), you cannot replace DDS with Pilot. You can, however, run Pilot alongside ROS2 for swarm-level coordination while keeping ROS2 for intra-robot communication.
The event stream is designed for coordination messages (telemetry, status updates, waypoints), not control loops. For servo commands or IMU fusion at 100+ Hz, use a dedicated real-time transport.
Release builds cover Linux and macOS on amd64 and arm64. Microcontrollers such as the ESP32 cannot run the daemon; bridge them through a companion computer.
Use ROS2 for intra-robot communication (sensors, actuators, navigation). Use Pilot for inter-robot communication (swarm telemetry, task assignment, coordination). Each layer does what it is good at.
Getting Started with a Robot Swarm
Set up a 3-robot swarm with a ground station and a hub:

fields.code:
# On every node: install pilotctl and pilot-daemon, then start the daemon
curl -fsSL https://pilotprotocol.network/install.sh | sh
pilotctl daemon start

# On the hub (always on): name it, then approve each node's handshake
pilotctl set-hostname swarm-hub
pilotctl pending
pilotctl approve <node_id>

# On the ground station
pilotctl set-hostname ground-station
pilotctl extras set-tags ground-station swarm-controller
pilotctl handshake <hub-address> "ground station for survey-team-alpha"
pilotctl subscribe <hub-address|hostname> swarm.telemetry

# On each robot (Raspberry Pi / Jetson with a 64-bit OS)
pilotctl set-hostname robot-01
pilotctl extras set-tags swarm-member robot ground-unit
pilotctl handshake <hub-address> "robot-01 in survey-team-alpha"

# Verify connectivity
pilotctl ping <hub-address|hostname>

# Start publishing telemetry
pilotctl publish <hub-address|hostname> swarm.telemetry --data '{"drone_id":"robot-01","lat":37.77,"lon":-122.42,"battery_pct":95}'

children.text: No ROS2 installation. No DDS configuration. No multicast tuning. Two binaries that run on 64-bit Linux ARM devices and provide encrypted, NAT-traversing swarm communication out of the box.
One UDP socket per daemon, no multicast storms. Coordinate robot swarms on constrained hardware with zero-configuration networking.
